channel.description: Recent content in Nlp on Best of AI

item.title: Baidu ERNIE
item.description:
ERNIE, which stands for Enhanced Representation through Knowledge Integration, is Baidu’s answer to ChatGPT. The consumer chatbot answers questions, writes and edits text, generates images, and handles tasks in Chinese and other languages, and it is built into Baidu’s search engine and apps. It benefits from Baidu’s knowledge graph and search data, and is a major option for Chinese-language users.

For developers and companies, Baidu offers ERNIE models through its Qianfan cloud platform, with APIs, fine-tuning, and tools for building AI applications. The company has released versions of its models with open weights, which lets developers run them independently. The models support multimodal inputs and reasoning, and are used in enterprise products, cloud services, and Baidu’s autonomous driving and other businesses.

item.title: Qlik
item.description: Qlik is known for its associative engine, which treats all the data in an app as connected. When you click a value in a chart, everything else updates to show related data, and values that are unrelated are shown as excluded, which helps users discover connections they did not think to query. This differs from tools that require predefined queries and has been a selling point for business users exploring data.

item.title: TypingMind
item.description:
TypingMind is a front end for AI models. A user supplies API keys, and gets a clean chat app with conversation folders, prompt libraries, and tools. Pay-per-use API pricing can be cheaper than several subscriptions, especially for light users.

Features include support for multiple models in one place, custom assistants, plugins, and knowledge uploads, and teams can share setups with controlled access. It is a paid product with a one-time or subscription license depending on the plan.

item.title: Enlive
item.description:
Enlive is a prompt layer. Instead of writing a long, careful prompt, a user types a brief request, and Enlive expands it with relevant context, structure, and instructions before sending it to a model. The idea is to get better answers from people who are not prompt engineers.

It works across multiple models and tracks preferences, such as tone and format, so later requests fit the user’s habits. This addresses the common experience that vague prompts return vague answers. For power users it can save the time spent rewriting prompts.

item.title: DeepSeek
item.description: DeepSeek is an AI research company based in China whose models are released with their weights open, so anyone can download, run, and fine-tune them. Its general-purpose models handle chat, writing, and coding, and its reasoning models work through a problem step by step before answering. What got the industry’s attention was efficiency: DeepSeek’s models perform near the best closed systems on many math and coding benchmarks while being far cheaper to train and serve. Its technical papers, which describe how it did this, are widely read by other labs.

item.title: DeepSeek Chat
item.description:
DeepSeek Chat offers consumer access to DeepSeek’s language models. Users ask questions, draft text, write code, and work through math and logic, and a mode shows the model’s step-by-step reasoning before it gives an answer. It supports uploading files and searching the web.

DeepSeek drew wide attention when its models matched strong Western systems at much lower reported training cost, and it released the model weights openly, which let others run and study them. The chat app was one of the most downloaded in many countries soon after it launched.

item.title: Gemini Pro
item.description: Gemini Pro refers to the mid-sized models in Google’s Gemini family, positioned between the smaller, cheaper Flash models and the heaviest reasoning options. Google’s naming moves with each generation, but the idea stays the same: Pro is the version intended for demanding everyday work without the cost or delay of the very largest model. Gemini was designed from the start to take in several types of input at once, so the same model reads text, looks at images, listens to audio, and watches video rather than handing those jobs to separate systems.

item.title: Mistral
item.description: Mistral is Europe’s best-known frontier AI lab. It first drew attention by releasing compact open-weight models that matched or beat larger ones, and it has continued to release models in several sizes for chat, coding, reasoning, and vision. Some are free to download under permissive licenses, while its strongest models are offered through its API and Le Chat. Developers like that it gives them the choice to run models on their own hardware.

item.title: Qwen Studio
item.description:
Qwen Studio is the consumer-facing way to use Alibaba’s Qwen models. Users chat with the assistant, search the web, upload documents and images for analysis, write code, and generate pictures and video. A mode shows the model’s reasoning for harder problems.

The Qwen family is notable for open-weight releases that developers can download and run, so Qwen Studio doubles as a showcase of what those models can do. It supports many languages, with strong coverage of Chinese and English.

item.title: BERT
item.description: BERT (Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers) is a language model that Google Research published in October 2018, and it changed how the field approached pretraining for NLP tasks. Unlike earlier models that read text left to right, BERT trains on masked-word prediction and next-sentence prediction, letting it build representations that draw on context from both directions at once. Google released two main sizes: BERT-base at 110 million parameters and BERT-large at 340 million, both with a 512-token limit, and made the weights freely available under Apache 2.0 on GitHub and later Hugging Face. Fine-tuned versions of BERT set new records on eleven different NLP benchmarks at launch, including question answering and natural language inference, and it quickly became the standard base model to fine-tune for tasks like classification, named entity recognition, and search ranking. It’s mostly been superseded by newer encoder models like RoBERTa and DeBERTa and by the embedding models that followed it, but it’s still one of the most cited papers in NLP and its architecture underlies a large share of later encoder-based systems.

item.title: Bloomfire
item.description:
Bloomfire is a knowledge management platform. Employees add articles, files, videos, and Q&A to a central library, tag them, and find them later with search. The platform is meant to hold what a company knows so that people do not keep asking colleagues the same questions.

AI features make retrieval easier. Users ask questions in plain language and get answers drawn from the company’s own content with links to sources, and the system can suggest related material and flag content that needs updating. Analytics show what people search for and where gaps exist.

item.title: Haystack
item.description:
Haystack helps developers assemble applications that answer questions over documents. A pipeline strings together components: converting files, splitting text, creating embeddings, retrieving relevant passages, and generating an answer with a language model. Each component is swappable, so teams can change a model or database without rewriting everything.

The framework supports many model providers and vector stores, hybrid search, evaluation tools, and agents that use tools. It also provides a way to serialize pipelines, which supports deployment and testing. deepset offers a commercial platform around it for companies that want managed hosting and collaboration.

item.title: Hex
item.description:
Hex combines notebooks with business intelligence. Teams connect their data warehouse, write SQL and Python in a notebook, and turn the results into interactive apps that non-technical colleagues can use without code. Everything lives in one place with version history and comments.

AI is built into the workflow. Magic helps write and fix queries and code, and agents let business users ask questions of governed data in plain language. A semantic layer keeps definitions of metrics consistent, so answers match across reports. Scheduled runs keep outputs fresh.

item.title: Landbot
item.description:
Landbot lets non-developers design conversations visually. A user drags blocks onto a canvas to ask questions, branch based on answers, and connect to other tools, then publishes the flow on a website, a landing page, or WhatsApp. The conversational format often gets more responses than a plain form.

AI features add the ability to answer free-text questions from a knowledge base and to build flows from a description. Integrations send leads to CRMs and spreadsheets, and handoff routes complex chats to human agents. Templates cover lead generation, support, and onboarding.

item.title: MotherDuck
item.description:
MotherDuck takes the DuckDB analytical database, which runs on a laptop, and adds a cloud service. A user connects from their local DuckDB, queries data in the cloud, and combines it with local files, in what the company calls hybrid execution, using each machine for what it does best.

It targets teams that do not need a large data warehouse. Features include shared databases, collaboration, integrations with common data tools, and an AI assistant that helps write SQL. The pitch is simple, fast analytics at lower cost for data in the gigabytes to terabytes range.

item.title: ScrapeGraph AI
item.description:
ScrapeGraph AI lets developers describe what they want from a page. A user supplies a URL and a prompt such as list every product name and price, and the library fetches the page, passes it to a language model, and returns structured data. It also builds graph pipelines for multi-page scraping.

The approach reduces the brittleness of selector-based scrapers, which break when layouts change. It supports local and cloud models, and a hosted API and no-code options exist.

item.title: Clarifai
item.description: Clarifai started as an image recognition API and has grown into a broader AI platform. Teams use it to find and call models for vision, language, and audio tasks, to train their own models on labeled data, and to run them in production. It includes tools for organizing and labeling data, searching images and video, and building workflows that chain several models together. Industries such as retail, media, and public sector have used it to classify content and find objects in large collections.

item.title: Lexalytics
item.description: Lexalytics builds natural language processing for businesses that need to make sense of large amounts of text. Its Salience engine reads reviews, survey comments, support tickets, social posts, and call transcripts and returns structured information: whether the sentiment is positive or negative, which products or people are mentioned, what themes recur, and what the author intends. Analysts can then count, trend, and compare these signals instead of reading comments one by one.

item.title: Stats Perform
item.description:
Stats Perform collects detailed data about professional sports. Trained collectors and tracking technology record events in matches, such as passes, shots, and player positions, and the company supplies that information to broadcasters, media companies, sportsbooks, leagues, and clubs. Its Opta brand is widely seen in football statistics on television and websites. The data feeds power live scores, fantasy games, and graphics.

AI is used both to create data and to analyze it. Computer vision extracts player and ball tracking from video, which reduces the manual work of collecting information, and models predict outcomes, evaluate player performance, and estimate the value of actions on the field. Coaches and analysts use the tools for scouting and tactical analysis, while media and betting clients use predictions and content such as automated match summaries.

item.title: Causal
item.description:
Causal was created for finance teams that outgrew spreadsheets. Users build models from blocks that represent revenue, headcount, and costs, link them to data from accounting and CRM systems, and see results as charts and dashboards. The structure makes models easier to follow and share than a sprawling workbook.

Scenario planning is a core strength. Teams can change assumptions, such as hiring plans or pricing, and compare outcomes side by side, then present the results to executives and investors. AI features help create models from descriptions and explain changes in numbers.

item.title: ChatGPT
item.description: ChatGPT is a chat interface to OpenAI’s language models. You type or speak a request and it answers in plain language, whether that means drafting an email, explaining a concept, debugging a function, or summarizing a long PDF. It can take images and files as input and generate images in return. For many people it is the first AI tool they ever used, and that familiarity is a big part of why it remains the default comparison for every other assistant.

item.title: Claap
item.description: Claap targets teams that want fewer live meetings. You can record your screen and camera as a short video, share a link, and let colleagues watch and respond on their own time. The same tool records live calls on Zoom, Google Meet, and Teams, then stores them with a transcript. Comments and reactions can be attached to specific moments, so feedback stays tied to the part of the video it refers to.

item.title: Claude
item.description: Claude is the AI assistant from Anthropic, a company that focuses on AI safety research. It comes in a few model tiers, with smaller and faster models for quick tasks and larger ones for harder reasoning and coding. People tend to pick it for writing that sounds less formulaic, careful reading of long documents, and code. It is also more willing than some competitors to say it is unsure or to disagree with you, which some users value and others find less accommodating.

item.title: Clockwise
item.description:
Clockwise worked inside Google Calendar and Slack to protect time for deep work. It looked at a team’s calendars, moved flexible meetings, and combined scattered gaps into longer blocks, aiming to cut the constant switching between tasks that fragments a workday. It could also find meeting times that worked for groups.

The product grew a following among engineering and product teams, and added AI scheduling features and a way to plan work around priorities. The company ended the service and the team joined Salesforce, where they work on AI agents. The product itself did not move over.

item.title: Gemini
item.description: Gemini is Google’s family of AI models and the assistant built on top of them. You can use it in the standalone Gemini app and website, but it also shows up inside the products many people already use: it can help draft emails in Gmail, rewrite text in Docs, summarize files in Drive, and answer questions on Android phones. If most of your work and personal life already runs on a Google account, that integration is the main reason to choose Gemini over another assistant.

item.title: Gemini Advanced
item.description:
Gemini Advanced was Google’s answer to ChatGPT Plus. When Google rebranded Bard as Gemini, it introduced Advanced as a subscription, sold through Google One, that gave access to its strongest model, longer conversations, and features like file uploads and integration with Gmail and Docs. It also bundled extra Google One storage, which made it attractive to people already paying for cloud storage.

Google later reorganized the plans. Gemini Advanced’s features moved into Google AI Pro, and a higher tier called Google AI Ultra provides the most advanced models, agent features, and generous limits for heavy users. The plans include perks such as video generation, deeper research tools, and integrations with Workspace apps, and the exact lineup changes with each product update.

item.title: GitLens AI
item.description:
GitLens enriches VS Code with Git history. It shows inline blame annotations that say who last changed a line, when, and in which commit, and lets you browse the history of a file, line, or branch without leaving the editor. Features include a commit graph, comparisons across branches, and a Launchpad that gathers pull requests and issues. It’s one of the most downloaded extensions for VS Code.

AI features help with common Git chores. GitLens can write commit messages from staged changes, summarize what a commit or branch changed in plain language, and help draft pull request descriptions, saving time on documentation. It supports several AI providers and models, with options for how data is sent.

item.title: GPT Engineer
item.description:
GPT Engineer was among the first projects to show that a language model could generate a whole working program from a prompt. A user wrote a specification, the tool asked clarifying questions, and then it produced files and code. The open-source command line version attracted a large community of developers.

The founders built a hosted product, gptengineer.app, that let non-programmers describe a web app and see it built. That product was renamed Lovable, which grew into one of the best-known AI app builders. The original open-source repository remains available as a way to experiment with prompt-to-code workflows.

item.title: Harvey
item.description:
Harvey was built for lawyers and has become one of the best-known legal AI companies. Attorneys use its assistant to ask legal questions, draft and revise contracts and memos, summarize documents, and analyze large sets of files, such as the documents in a due diligence review. It runs on leading language models adapted for legal work and is designed to provide citations so lawyers can verify the answers.

Beyond a chat assistant, Harvey offers structured features. Vault stores and analyzes large document collections, workflows automate multi-step tasks such as contract review against a playbook, and integrations connect with tools law firms already use, including document management and legal research providers. Firms can customize the system with their own templates and precedents, and security controls support the confidentiality requirements of legal practice.

item.title: IBM Watson Government
item.description:
IBM Watson Government packages IBM’s AI offerings for the public sector. Agencies use them for tasks such as analyzing large volumes of text, extracting information from documents, supporting citizen service chatbots, and detecting fraud or anomalies in data. The emphasis is on meeting security and compliance standards that governments require.

The services run on IBM’s cloud and in hybrid environments, with options for on-premises deployment. Newer watsonx products add generative AI and governance tools for tracking models and risks, which agencies need under rules for responsible AI.

item.title: Kasisto
item.description:
Kasisto builds AI assistants for banks. Its KAI technology understands banking questions and can carry out actions, such as showing recent transactions, transferring funds, or explaining a fee, in a chat within a bank’s mobile app or website. The language models are tuned to the vocabulary and rules of finance.

A newer product, KAI Answers, uses generative AI to answer questions from a bank’s own policies and documents, with citations so staff and customers can see the source. Banks use it to cut call volumes and improve self-service, and the company has worked with institutions around the world.

item.title: Kensho
item.description:
Kensho began as a startup applying machine learning to financial markets and was acquired by S&P Global, where it operates as the company’s AI innovation hub. Its products address practical data problems in finance. Kensho Link matches records between data sets, such as linking company names across different sources, Kensho Classify tags documents by category, and Kensho Extract pulls data out of PDFs and filings.

More recent work connects financial data to generative AI. Kensho develops tools that allow AI assistants and agents to access S&P Global’s data reliably, with grounding that provides sources for answers, plus language models and benchmarks for finance. Its technology supports S&P products and is available to clients who want to build their own applications.

item.title: Kimi
item.description:
Kimi first gained attention for handling very long documents. Users can upload large PDFs, books, or collections of files and ask questions, and the assistant keeps track of the whole text, which suited tasks like summarizing reports and analyzing contracts. It also searches the web, writes and reasons about code, and has agent features that carry out multi-step tasks.

Moonshot AI releases powerful models, including open-weight versions of its Kimi K2 family, which are among the larger open models and strong at coding and agentic tasks. Developers use them through Moonshot’s API or run them through third-party providers, and they are often used inside coding tools. The company competes with other Chinese labs such as DeepSeek, Alibaba, and Zhipu.

item.title: LangChain
item.description: LangChain gave developers a common toolkit when language models first became available through APIs. It supplies building blocks for the typical parts of an AI application: calling a model, formatting prompts, parsing outputs, connecting to tools and data sources, and keeping memory of a conversation. Because it supports many model providers and vector stores behind consistent interfaces, you can swap one for another with little code change. Python and JavaScript versions are available.

item.title: Le Chat
item.description:
Le Chat is Mistral’s answer to ChatGPT and Claude. The French company designed the app for general use: answering questions, writing and editing, summarizing documents, analyzing images, generating images, and running code. Fast response modes make it quick for everyday queries, and a canvas supports working on documents and code beside the chat.

Further features address more advanced needs. Deep research compiles longer reports from web sources, connectors link to services like Gmail, Google Drive, and Notion, and custom agents let users set up specialized assistants. Memory can retain preferences between chats, and mobile apps bring it to phones. The assistant uses Mistral’s own models, some of which are open-weight, and emphasizes European hosting and privacy options.

item.title: Morningstar AI
item.description:
Morningstar is known for independent research on funds, stocks, and markets. Its star ratings for mutual funds and ETFs became a standard reference, and analysts publish research and fair value estimates on companies. Individual investors use its website and premium subscriptions to screen investments and build portfolios, while advisors and institutions use products like Morningstar Direct for deeper analysis, portfolio construction, and reporting.

AI has been added to make research easier to navigate. Mo is a conversational assistant that answers investing questions using Morningstar’s research and data, summarizes reports, and explains concepts, with an emphasis on drawing from the company’s own vetted content to limit errors. Other uses include automated summaries of earnings calls and analyst notes, and data tools that help build screens and analyze holdings.

item.title: Mosaic
item.description:
Mosaic is aimed at finance teams that want a modern view of the business. It pulls data from accounting systems, sales tools, and HR platforms into a single model, so metrics like revenue, headcount, and cash are current and consistent. Teams build reports and board decks from live data.

Forecasting and scenario tools let teams test assumptions, such as hiring plans or pricing changes, and see the impact. AI allows users to ask questions in plain language and get analysis, and automates routine commentary and variance explanations.

item.title: NeuralText
item.description:
NeuralText is an SEO content suite. Users find keywords, group them into clusters by intent, study what ranks for a term, and create content briefs that list topics and questions to cover. The AI writer then drafts articles or sections using those guidelines.

The tool aims to let one person handle research, planning, and drafting. A content editor scores text against the brief, and additional templates cover ads, product descriptions, and social posts.

item.title: OpenHands
item.description:
OpenHands provides an open alternative to commercial coding agents. A user gives it a task, and the agent works in a sandbox with a terminal, an editor, and a browser, taking steps to complete the job and showing its work. It can resolve GitHub issues and open pull requests.

The project started as OpenDevin, an open-source response to the Devin demo, and grew into a community-driven platform run by All Hands AI. It supports models from many providers, has a command line tool and a web interface, and is used in research and benchmarks for coding agents.

item.title: Perplexity
item.description: Perplexity works more like a search engine than a chatbot. You ask a question, it searches the web in real time, and it writes a short answer with numbered citations you can click to check. That makes it good for current events, product comparisons, and fact-finding where you need to see where the information came from. Follow-up questions keep the context, and you can narrow searches to sources like academic papers or forums.

item.title: Perplexity AI
item.description:
Perplexity positions itself as an alternative to the list of links. You ask a question in natural language, it searches the web in real time, reads the pages, and writes a concise answer with citations to each source. That format is helpful for questions where you want a quick overview with a way to check the evidence, such as product comparisons, news, how-to questions, and research basics.

The experience supports continued exploration. Follow-up questions build on earlier context, and focus options narrow the search to categories such as academic sources or discussion forums. Pro Search runs more steps for complex questions, and Deep Research generates longer reports. The Comet browser brings the assistant into everyday browsing, and Spaces organize related research. Users can choose among several models in paid plans.

item.title: PitchBook
item.description:
PitchBook tracks private markets. Its database covers companies, funding rounds, investors, funds, acquisitions, and valuations, and analysts use it to find targets, benchmark deals, and research sectors. Reports and data feeds support investment decisions and strategy work.

AI tools help users query the database in natural language, summarize companies and markets, and speed up research tasks. Integrations with Excel and CRM systems bring data into daily workflows. The company also publishes market research.

item.title: Poe
item.description:
Poe gives access to many AI models without separate accounts. A single app and website lets you switch between leading chatbots, image generators, and video tools, compare answers, and keep your conversations in one place. This is helpful for people who want to try different models and use whichever works best for each task.

Creators can build bots on top of models with custom prompts and knowledge, and publish them for others, with ways to earn revenue based on usage. The platform also offers an app builder and an API so developers can use Poe’s models in their projects. Group chats let multiple bots and people interact in one conversation.

item.title: Railway
item.description:
Railway makes hosting feel easy. A developer connects a GitHub repository, and Railway detects the language, builds the app, and runs it, with databases like Postgres, Redis, and MySQL added in a click. Environments, variables, and networking are managed in a visual canvas.

Usage-based pricing and preview environments suit small teams, startups, and side projects. Many AI app builders and hobbyists use it to deploy back ends quickly. Features include cron jobs, volumes for storage, and private networking.

item.title: Retool AI
item.description:
Retool is designed for engineers who need to build internal software quickly. Developers connect databases, APIs, and services, drag components such as tables, forms, and charts onto a canvas, and write queries and logic in SQL and JavaScript where needed. The result is an application for operations, support, or finance teams to manage data, approve requests, or run workflows, built in hours instead of weeks.

AI is integrated across the platform. A generative assistant can create an app from a description, write queries, and generate components, and Retool offers AI actions to classify, summarize, and extract information as parts of apps and workflows. Retool Agents let teams build agents that use their data and tools, and workflows automate scheduled and event-driven tasks. Enterprise controls cover permissions, audit logs, and self-hosting.

item.title: Scale AI
item.description:
Scale AI built its business on a simple observation: AI models need huge amounts of well-labeled data, and quality control at scale is hard. It combines software with a large network of human contributors and experts to annotate images, video, text, and sensor data. Early customers included self-driving car developers, and the company grew by supplying training data to the biggest AI labs.

Today much of its work involves large language models. Scale provides human feedback data used in reinforcement learning, expert-written examples for fine-tuning, and evaluations that test models for accuracy and safety. Its tools help companies manage data pipelines, and a generative AI platform lets enterprises customize models on their own data. Public-sector work includes AI systems for defense and government agencies, and the company runs public leaderboards that rank models on hard tests.

item.title: Scalenut
item.description:
Scalenut combines SEO research with AI writing. A user enters a keyword, and the platform analyzes search results to suggest topics, questions, and structure, then produces an outline and draft article, optimized for search. A one-click mode called Cruise creates a full article by following the steps of research, outline, and writing automatically.

Other features support content marketing. A keyword planner clusters terms into topics, an optimization score guides edits, and tools help with rewriting, product descriptions, and social content. The platform includes brand voice settings, a plagiarism checker, and a feature for tracking content performance. Teams can collaborate and manage projects in the app.

item.title: ServiceNow
item.description:
ServiceNow began as an IT service management tool and became a general workflow platform for large organizations. Employees and customers submit requests, such as a laptop problem, a payroll question, or a customer complaint, and the platform routes, tracks, and resolves them using defined workflows. Companies use it as a system of record and action across IT operations, HR, legal, security, and customer service.

AI is central to its current strategy. Now Assist adds generative AI to summarize cases, draft replies, and help agents find answers, and AI agents can take on tasks such as triaging incidents and fulfilling requests with minimal human intervention. The company acquired Moveworks, whose employee assistant is intended to become the front door to the platform, and offers tools to govern and monitor agents across the enterprise.

item.title: Shortwave
item.description:
Shortwave is a Gmail client that rethinks the inbox. Related messages are grouped into threads, newsletters and receipts can be bundled so they do not clutter the main view, and snooze, scheduling, and split inboxes help you process email faster. It works on Mac, Windows, iOS, Android, and the web, and connects to your Gmail account.

AI is central. You can ask the assistant questions about your email, such as what a client asked for last month or when a trip was booked, and it searches and answers using your messages. It summarizes long threads, drafts replies in your tone, and can take actions like organizing, labeling, and scheduling. The goal is to cut the time spent finding and writing.

item.title: Sisense
item.description:
Sisense helps organizations analyze data and share insights. Analysts connect data sources, build models and dashboards, and users explore results in a browser. Its strength is embedding: software companies place Sisense charts and analytics inside their products for customers.

AI features include asking questions in plain language, forecasting, and automatic detection of unusual patterns, plus a generative assistant that builds dashboards. The platform works with cloud data warehouses and offers an API-first approach.

item.title: Smartsheet AI
item.description:
Smartsheet is built around the grid. Teams manage projects, requests, and processes in sheets that look like spreadsheets but add features such as attachments, comments, dependencies, and approvals. The same data can be viewed as a Gantt chart, calendar, board, or form, and reports and dashboards summarize progress for leaders. It’s used for project plans, marketing calendars, intake processes, and portfolio tracking in many large organizations.

Automation and AI reduce manual work. Rules can send alerts, request approvals, or update fields when conditions are met, and AI helps by generating formulas from plain language, summarizing sheets, creating content, and analyzing data to find trends. Newer features allow building workflows and agents with natural language. Integrations connect with Microsoft 365, Google Workspace, Slack, Salesforce, and more.

item.title: Tray.io
item.description:
Tray.io builds on the idea of integration-platform-as-a-service. Teams use a visual builder to create workflows that connect SaaS applications, databases, and internal systems, with powerful logic, error handling, and the ability to write code where necessary. Hundreds of connectors and a universal connector for APIs cover common enterprise tools such as Salesforce, Workday, and Slack.

The company has moved toward AI agents. Its Merlin AI tools let teams build agents that use the connected systems as tools, so an agent can look up a customer, update a record, and send a message, with governance over what it can access. Embedded integration products let software companies offer customer-facing integrations in their own products.

item.title: Venice AI
item.description: Venice AI builds its pitch around privacy and freedom of use. The company states it does not log or store conversations on its servers, and that chats are kept in the user’s browser, which appeals to people uneasy about their prompts being retained or used for training. It runs open-source models, so users can pick from several language models and an image generator, and the platform applies fewer content restrictions than many mainstream services.

item.title: Warp
item.description:
Warp rethinks the command line interface. Each command and its output appear as a block that you can copy, share, search, or collapse, and the input behaves like a text editor with cursor movement, multiple cursors, and autocomplete. That makes the terminal friendlier to people who find traditional shells unforgiving, without removing the shell itself.

AI is built in. You can type a request in plain language and get the matching command, ask why an error happened, and hand longer tasks to an agent that plans steps, runs commands with your approval, and fixes problems as they come up. Warp Drive stores saved commands and workflows that teams can share, and the terminal also works with other coding agents running inside it.

item.title: Wordsmith
item.description:
Wordsmith turns data into text. Users define templates and logic, connect a data source, and the platform writes a narrative for each record, such as a financial summary, a sports recap, or a personalized report. The output is consistent and can be produced in volume.

It predates today’s chat models. Rule-based natural language generation gives predictable text, which suits regulated reporting where exact control matters, while large language models offer flexibility and fluency but less predictability.

item.title: Workato
item.description:
Workato is an integration and automation platform. Teams build recipes that link applications such as Salesforce, Workday, and Slack, trigger actions, and move data. Business users can create simple automations while IT governs the platform.

The company has added AI across the product. Users describe a workflow in plain language and Workato builds a draft, document understanding extracts data, and agents handle tasks with enterprise controls. Governance, security, and monitoring suit regulated companies.

item.title: 01.AI
item.description:
01.AI started with the goal of building leading large language models. Its Yi series, released with open weights, performed strongly on benchmarks for its size and supported long context and Chinese and English. Developers around the world downloaded and fine-tuned the models, and the company also offered an API and consumer products. Kai-Fu Lee, a well-known AI executive and investor, led the company.

The company’s strategy changed as the cost of competing at the frontier rose and powerful open models from other Chinese labs became available. It reduced its investment in pretraining its own large models and moved toward selling AI solutions to businesses, using other models where appropriate. Reports describe a focus on enterprise data infrastructure and a path toward a public listing.

item.title: Aleph Alpha
item.description: Aleph Alpha was Europe’s attempt to build a homegrown large language model company. Its Luminous models offered multilingual text generation and could handle images alongside text, with an emphasis on explainability, so users could see which parts of a source supported an answer. The company pitched itself to public sector agencies, banks, and industrial companies in Europe that wanted AI under their own control and in line with European regulation.

item.title: ContractPodAi
item.description:
ContractPodAi was built for corporate legal departments that handle large volumes of contracts. Its platform covers the lifecycle: drafting from templates, routing for approval, negotiation, signature, storage in a searchable repository, and tracking of obligations and renewals. It connects with systems such as Salesforce, Microsoft 365, and ERP tools so contracts sit within the business processes they relate to.

The company has rebranded as Leah, after the name of its AI product, and now describes itself as an agentic AI platform. Its AI agents review contracts against playbooks, flag risks and deviations, extract key terms, answer questions about a contract portfolio, and handle repetitive tasks across legal, procurement, and finance. The change reflects a wider move in legal technology from software that stores documents to software that does the first pass of the work.

item.title: Convai
item.description:
Convai makes game characters that respond to what players say. A developer defines a character’s personality, backstory, and knowledge, and Convai handles listening to speech, generating replies with a language model, speaking them with a synthetic voice, and driving lip sync and gestures. Plugins integrate with Unity, Unreal Engine, and other platforms.

Characters can also take actions in the game world, such as navigating or interacting with objects, based on conversation. Use cases include immersive games, training simulations, virtual tours, and educational experiences where open-ended dialogue adds value over scripted lines.

item.title: Fantastical
item.description:
Fantastical is known for natural language entry. A user types a phrase such as lunch with Sam next Tuesday at noon, and the app creates the event with the right time, place, and attendees. It shows calendars from many accounts in one view, including Google, iCloud, and Exchange, along with tasks and reminders.

Scheduling features help with coordination. Users can share availability and let others book time, propose several slots to a group, and attach video conference details automatically. Newer AI features help with preparation for meetings and smart suggestions, and the app integrates with other tools through its calendar sets and openings.

item.title: Klevu
item.description:
Klevu improves how online shoppers find products. Instead of matching keywords exactly, its search engine uses natural language processing to interpret queries, handle synonyms and misspellings, and rank results based on relevance and merchandising goals. It works with platforms such as Shopify, Magento, and BigCommerce.

The product also includes category browsing, recommendations, and analytics on what shoppers search for and fail to find. Merchandisers can adjust results with rules, and AI personalization adapts to a shopper’s behavior. A chat-style assistant answers product questions.

item.title: Nous Research
item.description:
Nous Research started as a group of researchers and hobbyists working in the open. Its Hermes models fine-tune open base models to follow instructions, use tools, and handle roleplay and reasoning, and have been popular among people running models locally. Data, methods, and weights are shared publicly.

The group has also worked on decentralized training, exploring ways to train large models across many machines run by different parties, and on tooling for agents. It operates as a company and offers access to its models through an API and an agent product.

item.title: Wordware
item.description:
Wordware treats prompts as code. Users write workflows in an editor that feels like a document, mixing instructions in plain language with structure for loops, branches, and tool calls. The aim is to let people who understand a problem, not only engineers, build AI apps.

Workflows can be published as apps or APIs, and the platform supports several model providers and integrations. Teams use it for research agents, content workflows, and internal tools.

item.title: Aider
item.description: Aider is a command-line tool for pair programming with a language model. You start it inside a git repository, add the files you want to work on, and describe what you want in plain English. It edits the files directly, shows the diff, and commits each change with a sensible message, so you can review or undo anything the model did with ordinary git commands. That tight git integration is what makes it feel safe to use on a real project.

item.title: Character.ai
item.description: Character.AI lets you chat with an enormous catalog of AI personalities. Some are based on fictional characters or historical figures, many are invented by users, and you can build your own by writing a description of who the character is and how they talk. The results feel more like acting than answering questions: the characters stay in persona, remember what you have said in the conversation, and respond in a distinctive voice. Users spend long sessions on it, using it for role-play, story writing, language practice, and casual company.

item.title: ChatPlayground AI
item.description:
ChatPlayground addresses a simple question: which model is best for this task? Instead of opening several chatbots in separate tabs, a user types a prompt once and sees answers from multiple models side by side, including offerings from OpenAI, Google, Anthropic, DeepSeek, and open models.

That helps with writing, coding, and research tasks where quality varies by model. Users can save conversations, keep prompts organized, and switch between models while working. For people who pay for several subscriptions, a single place can be convenient.

item.title: Grok
item.description: Grok is the chatbot from xAI, Elon Musk’s AI company. It is built into X, so you can ask it about a post, a trending topic, or a thread without leaving the feed, and it is also available as a separate app and at grok.com. Its main distinguishing feature is live access to posts on X, which makes it unusually quick at summarizing what people are saying about a breaking story. The tone is a little looser than other assistants, and it will answer some questions that more cautious tools decline.

item.title: LlamaIndex
item.description: LlamaIndex started as an open-source library for connecting language models to private data, and that remains its core job. It helps load information from files, databases, APIs, and apps such as Notion and Slack, split it into pieces, index it, and retrieve the relevant parts when a user asks a question. This retrieval-augmented generation pattern is how many company chatbots answer from internal documents instead of from the model’s general knowledge.

item.title: Microsoft Copilot
item.description: Microsoft uses the Copilot name for a family of assistants rather than one product. The consumer Copilot app and website work like other AI chatbots: you can ask questions, generate text and images, talk by voice, and have it look at your screen or camera for help with what you are doing. It is built into Windows and the Edge browser, where it can summarize pages, compare information across open tabs, and help with tasks as you browse.

item.title: NovelAI
item.description: NovelAI started as a tool for writers who wanted an AI collaborator for fiction. In its editor, you write a passage and the AI continues it, with controls for style, memory, and the characters and world in your story. Features such as lorebooks store details about characters and places so the AI keeps them consistent, and you can edit, retry, and steer the output freely. It’s used by hobbyist novelists, roleplayers, and fan fiction writers.

item.title: Recall
item.description:
Recall acts as a personal archive that organizes itself. A user saves a web page, YouTube video, podcast, or document with a browser extension or app, and Recall produces a summary, extracts key points, and links the item to related content already in the library through a knowledge graph.

An assistant lets users ask questions across everything they have saved, and spaced repetition quizzes help them remember material. It suits people who consume a lot of information and lose track of it.
